rows.description: A private, brief message such as "That got out of hand. Can we talk tomorrow, just us?" moves the argument out of the audience. Speaking face to face, away from the group, removes most of the fuel.

next stage: Owning your part, not the whole

rows.subtype: Stage 6: Owning your part, not the whole [Response]
rows.description: Each says what they regret without demanding the other apologise first. A mature repair keeps friendship above who started it, and the group cools when the two of them do.
graph_context: previous stage: One person moves first

rows.subtype: Stage 1: Spark over a small thing [Actor]
rows.description: A flatmate finds dishes piled up for the third day and mutters a sarcastic remark. The dishes are not the real issue; it is a feeling of not being respected that has been building quietly.
graph_context: next stage: Defensive reply

rows.description: The other flatmate hears an attack on his character and answers with a list of what he has already done. He is protecting his self-image, so the complaint becomes a trial rather than a request.

rows.description: Statements become "you just don't care" and "you think you are better than us". Each person assigns motives to the other and hears them as fact, which makes any denial sound like another lie.
graph_context: previous stage: Defensive reply

rows.subtype: Stage 4: Peak and point of no return [Actor]
rows.description: A cruel remark lands on a known sore spot, such as money, family or failure. Both feel a flash of shame and anger, and some part of them knows it was too far but pride blocks taking it back.

rows.description: One person says "I am too angry to talk well; can we continue in an hour?" and actually returns. A stated pause with a return time is very different from storming off, which reads as punishment.
graph_context: previous stage: Peak and point of no return

rows.subtype: Stage 6: Repair and one concrete agreement [Response]
rows.description: On returning, each restates the other's point before their own and owns their harshest words. They leave with one small practical agreement, like a rota, because a shared plan holds better than a shared feeling.
graph_context: previous stage: Calling a time-out

rows.description: One partner feels the relationship slipping and craves reassurance and a proper talk. Underneath is fear of being left, though it comes out as questions, hints and a sharper tone than intended.

rows.description: She sends several messages and asks "what is wrong with us?" the moment he walks in. She believes closeness is on the other side of the conversation, so more pressing feels like the only way to reach him.
